title: When Your Original Thesis Is Wrong, Pay To Fix It Fast
documentTitle: FTC v. Meta Platforms, Inc. — Exhibit PX1102
excerptForBlog:
I wonder if we should consider buying Instagram, even if it costs ~$500m.

Right now they seem to have two things that we don't: a really good camera and a photo-centric sharing network.

For the camera piece, their camera just takes photos that look much nicer than the native camera because of their filters, tilt-shift effects and even their new lux feature. I worry that it will take us too long to catch up, if we even will. And regardless, their brand is established as the awesome mainstream camera, so even if we catch up on features they're still the awesome iPhone camera app.

For the network piece, one concerning trend is that a huge number of people are using Instagram every day — including everyone ranging from non-technical high school friends to even FB employees — and they're only uploading some of their photos to FB. This creates a huge hole for us.

I think it's quite possible that our initial thesis was wrong and that theirs is right — that what people want is more to take the best photos than to put them on FB. If so, we'd be very behind in both functionality and brand on how one of the core use cases of Facebook will evolve in the mobile world, which is really scary and why we might want to consider paying a lot of money for this.

lessonTitle: When Your Original Thesis Is Wrong, Pay To Fix It Fast
pullQuote: If a small competitor has already won the use case your future depends on, the cheapest option is usually to buy them — before the market figures out how valuable they are.
leadershipTraits: Reads competitors through user behavior, not press
situation: On February 11, 2012, Mark Zuckerberg wrote an internal note floating the idea of acquiring Instagram for roughly $500 million. Instagram had two things Facebook lacked: better photo quality and a photo-first sharing network. Zuckerberg was deciding whether to build, ignore, or buy.
insight:
The surface read is 'Facebook wanted a better camera.' The deeper move is more significant. Zuckerberg wrote that 'our initial thesis was wrong' — that people might want to take great photos more than they want to post them to Facebook. That's not a feature gap. That's a use-case gap. If Instagram's model was right, Facebook's core mobile story would be built on a flawed assumption. He was staring at disruptive innovation from below: a simpler, focused product pulling users away from a more complex one, starting with photos.

He also named a brand problem that features alone couldn't fix: 'even if we catch up on features they're still the awesome iPhone camera app.' Catching up technically wouldn't reclaim the position. The $500 million wasn't just buying code — it was buying the narrative before it hardened against Facebook.
application: Once a quarter, look at what your fastest-growing competitor is proving that you assumed wasn't true. If they're winning on a different thesis — not just better execution of yours — that's the signal to act. Don't ask 'can we build this?' Ask 'if they're right and we're wrong, what does that cost us in two years?' Price the answer honestly, then decide whether to build, partner, or acquire before the brand story sets.
